AI-assisted judging was used at the recent World Gymnastics Championships

Gymnastics is leading the way in applying artificial intelligence to the judging of elite sport, and it could be used to help decide medals at the LA Olympics.

Bosses in the sport said they would be "highly surprised" if AI-assisted judging was not implemented at the Games in 2028.

This is despite some leading gymnasts criticising its use at the recent World Championships, saying they were "not robots" and warning it could be "dangerous".

Olympic champion Carlos Yulo and British gymnast Harry Hepworth had the difficulty rating of their vaults downgraded in qualifying.

Both were performing the piked Dragulescu and had their scores reduced from a 5.6 to a 5.2.

They attempted the same vault in the final with Hepworth finishing sixth, while Yulo fell and came seventh.

On his return from Rotterdam, Hepworth told BBC Sport: "On the half twist I bend my legs so that I can prepare for the landing, which I think is the most sensible thing to do because you don't want to break your legs or anything.

"But the AI detection system caught on to it and said I was doing a tuck position, which then downgrades the vault by four tenths.

"It definitely cost me a few positions, I think, in the final for sure."

Referencing Yulo's experience, he said: "I think it does say a lot when me, the Olympic bronze medallist on vault, and the Olympic champion on vault are getting done by the AI system for the exact same thing.

"In the final he really did go for the straight legs and it just made him fall because it's just really hard to do, and I think quite dangerous as well."

Yulo said he was disappointed with the downgrading.

"I don't know what the problem is," he told Inside Gymnastics. "It's AI, I'm not a robot, we're human beings, in my eyes and in my opinion. I think everyone also is maybe a bit disappointed about it because everyone is feeling it is pike position, why is it only 5.2?"

Andrew Tombs, president of the Men's Artistic Gymnastics technical committee, believes the AI system can guarantee fairness for athletes and that is what they deserve.

He said judges at the World Championships would have downgraded the difficulty rating - even without using the Judging Support System (JSS).

But he did acknowledge lessons had been learned and that conversations were ongoing with coaches about the point at which the JSS should take its measurements.

"I think the decisions made at the championships were correct based on what was in the system," he added.

The JSS is an AI-powered technology that has been being developed by Fujitsu since 2017.

It uses advanced AI and motion analysis to recognise gymnastic elements, as well as providing multi-angle video reviews and objective numerical information on gymnasts' movements for the judges to use when considering their scores.

More than 800 elements have been programmed into the system, including the relevant parameter requirements such as body positions, angles in shoulders and bent legs.

"If you think about a body position between being straight and being piked, the differential could be one degree," Tombs explained.

"And when you get to a real marginal decision, the JSS system is there to support the judges making the right decision on those body angles particularly.

"It is a significant transformation for us in terms of how we judge our sport. It's been a long time in the making and we came away from Rotterdam really happy with how the system worked."

He said improvements were continuously being made.

"We've already started discussions with a couple of coaches in terms of understanding biomechanically the right moment at which that assessment is made," Tombs said.

"We're going to fine-tune, potentially, the point at which the leg measurement is made. So I think we'll make the sensible decisions going forward that will give a little bit more flexibility and adapt where we are today."

Hepworth said he can see the benefits of the JSS, but wants to see refinements made.

"It does sort of make you think, 'oh, what is the point in doing these crazy hard vaults' if you're just going to get it downgraded anyway? Like, is there actually a point?" he said.

"But I think if they do refine it, I think it'll be a brilliant tool. So hopefully going forward, it'll be all right."

Judged Olympic disciplines like dressage, freestyle skiing and snowboarding are exploring potential AI assistance.

The primary goals appear to be the pursuit of enhanced fairness, accuracy and integrity, and the elimination of ambiguity and subjectivity.

They also want to make judged sports easier to follow for audiences, as opposed to the current system where viewers tuning in once every four years might not understand why one athlete has won gold and another has finished off the podium.

The governing bodies for equestrian sports, skiing and snowboarding are poised to begin pilot projects on how AI can assist with judging.

In winter sports this will begin by testing the AI algorithms and technology at the top level of aerials skiing in 'coexistence' with human judges, before a wider rollout to other disciplines like halfpipe, slopestyle and big air if that is successful.

AI judging will be piloted in aerials skiing this season

The FEI - the world governing body for equestrian sports - is exploring how AI could be used within dressage judging, and will start trialling it in World Cups.

But some limitations have already been identified - namely because dressage involves judging the horse, the rider and the connection between them. Equestrian bosses told the BBC they believe there will always be a role for human judges.

"Judging is not just about whether a movement has been performed technically correct, or in the right place or at the right time," said Ronan Murphy, the FEI's dressage director.

"But it's also about the quality of that movement, the harmony between the horse and the athlete. Those are other characteristics which AI hasn't the ability to assess for us."

It could additionally be used to help enhance welfare checks during dressage competitions, for example by assessing whether a horse's nose line is consistently moving behind the vertical.

"I think that the technology could potentially support the review of observations relevant to horse wellbeing," he said.

"But any application like that would need rigorous validation, and appropriate veterinary expertise."

Murphy said that it is "very difficult" to answer whether AI-assisted judging will be in use by LA28.

"If we can satisfy ourselves that there is a technological benefit to use of artificial intelligence, then certainly we would be open to bringing that to the Olympic Games and all major championships," he said.

Within winter sports, BBC Sport was told the driver is fairness and removing bias, but also a push to make judging faster.

Urs Lehmann, secretary general of the International Ski Federation (FIS), said he wants AI to reduce the lag time between athletes.

He said he had recently measured the judging time in aerials, and that it took an average of one minute 45 seconds per athlete.

"[We want] the judging being done within 15 to 20 seconds max, so that we can increase the frequency of the athletes, which is the show," he said.

"We think AI is going to be more precise. No emotions, no influence by cheering crowds.

"The goal is that within three years from now, which would be in 2029, we would be ready for all, or at least a major part of our disciplines to go out with AI judging."

AI 'here to stay' at Artistic World Championships

World Gymnastics president Morinari Watanabe has openly said his dream was to have only computers and AI awarding scores in the future.

In response, Tombs said removing human judges was a long way off even being considered.

"Mori is a visionary," he said. "He's pushing gymnastics forward. He's trying to evolve what we do as a sport. Gymnastics has a massive peak at the Olympic Games.

"We need to make our sport more visible. We also need to make our sport more transparent, and the integrity of the sport has to improve.

"And I think JSS and real-time judging will do that.

"[But] I think it's a long way off for us at the moment."

David Beckham was knighted by King Charles in 2025

David Beckham will be inducted into the United States' National Soccer Hall of Fame as part of its 2027 class.

The former Manchester United and England midfielder, 51, made headlines in 2007 when he moved to Los Angeles from Spanish giants Real Madrid to join Major League Soccer (MLS) side LA Galaxy on a five-year contract.

He made 124 appearances in all competitions for Galaxy, scoring 20 goals, and twice won both the MLS Cup and Supporters' Shield.

Beckham's six seasons at Galaxy helped to raise the global profile of MLS and following his retirement in 2013, he became co-owner of MLS club Inter Miami, who signed Argentina World Cup winner Lionel Messi in 2023.

His induction ceremony is set to take place on 16 April 2027 in Frisco, Texas.

David Beckham's deal with LA Galaxy in 2007 was reportedly worth £128m

He was told the news he had been chosen on the veterans' ballot at an MLS board of governors' meeting on Thursday and said his time in the US has been "an incredible journey".

Beckham, who had two loan spells with AC Milan in 2009 and 2010 while at Galaxy, added: "I'm looking to build this league and this sport in this great country for a long time."

Meanwhile, former US internationals Megan Rapinoe and Julie Ertz have also been voted into the Hall of Fame in their first year of eligibility.

Ballon d'Or winner Rapinoe, 41, and midfielder Ertz, 34, lifted the Women’s World Cup twice with with the US in 2015 and 2019.

"To be alongside all the greatest players that have played for us, and played for our country alongside a bunch of my team-mates and friends, recognised like that in this way just means you were successful and a part of great teams," Rapinoe wrote on Instagram.

Northern Ireland have a number of options to pick from against Ukraine, who they beat 3-0 in the first fixture

After an impressive quadruple-header to kick off the Nations League, Northern Ireland are back in action and it's time for you to be the boss.

Michael O'Neill's young side did not concede a goal as away victories over Georgia and Ukraine were joined by two goalless draws at home to Hungary and the Georgians, which leave Northern Ireland top of League B2 after four matches.

Now, they will look to finish the job and earn promotion to League A as Ukraine visit Belfast on Saturday, before a trip to Hungary on Tuesday to close out the group.

But who would you pick if you were in charge of Northern Ireland? Weigh up some of the key selection dilemmas before having your say.

NI can draw on strong club form in key window

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

Of the 54 teams in the Nations League, Northern Ireland are the only side yet to concede a goal after four rounds of matches.

It's all the more impressive when you consider O'Neill is without two Premier League level defenders, in the form of Liverpool's Conor Bradley, a long-term absentee, and Daniel Ballard, who was injured in the first match of the campaign in Georgia in September.

O'Neill has a plethora of options, both at the heart of defence and out wide.

At centre-back, youngsters Tom Atcheson and Ruairi McConville impressed in the quadruple-header, while O'Neill could also utilise the experience of Paddy McNair or Ciaron Brown.

There are also several options at right-back, with Trai Hume, the in-form Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer - who can also play at left-back along with Justin Devenny - all available.

In goal, first-choice Pierce Charles has fresh competition in the shape of Manchester United stopper Dermot Mee.

Who would you pick to keep the run of clean sheets going?

Trai Hume has often been deployed as a right winger by Sunderland this season

Trai Hume has become something of a Swiss army knife option for both Northern Ireland and at Sunderland with his versatility.

Usually a right-back, Hume has often been utilised further forward on the right wing by Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris this season.

For Northern Ireland, the 24-year-old has played right across the defensive line when called upon.

With Conor Bradley fit and on the right flank, Hume would often feature as the right of three centre-backs, but he has also been deployed in both full-back positions.

Then, in October, he started in the centre of midfield against Ukraine and did not look out of place with a composed performance in a 3-0 win.

His versatility can only be a positive for Northern Ireland, but where would you play him to get the best out of both player and team?

Finding the back of the net has long been an issue for Northern Ireland, and despite the huge promise of this young team, they do still lack an out-and-out goalscorer.

Jamie Donley has been tasked with leading the line in recent matches, and he has been in good form at club level for Luton Town, albeit in a different role to the one his fills at international level.

His Luton team-mate Callum Marshall is another attacking option, and he can also be used out wide.

Josh Magennis is more of a target man option as he closes in on a century of Northern Ireland caps, while, at the other end of the experience scale, Braiden Graham is on the fringes of the first team with Everton and Eoin Kenny is untested having played just one Championship fixture since joining Portsmouth from Dundalk.

MN202611_hodw296sj3.t:
Pat Cummins spent over an hour fielding questions over sandpapergate on Friday

As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.

Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.

"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."

A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.

Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."

"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Josh says he was surprised the scandal is back in the news

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.

There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.

"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.

"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."

Khawaja has said he owed it to the three players punished to tell his side of the story

Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.

In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.

"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."

However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.

David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.

But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.

And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.

Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".

"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.

"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."

He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.

He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.

"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.

Australia kicked off it's summer with an ODI against England on Friday

Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.

"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."

"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.

"I don't know what the outcome will be."

When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.

Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.

Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.

One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.

During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.

Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.

For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.

I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.

When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.

We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.

Michael Carrick was sacked by Manchester United this week, but the club opened talks with Mauricio Pochettino before Carrick's departure was decided or confirmed

When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.

One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.

During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.

When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!

Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.

My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.

I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.

I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.

Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.

I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.

That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.

As a player, Burrows helped third-tier Swindon Town shock Arsenal in the 1969 League Cup final. As a manager, he had spells in charge of Portsmouth, Cardiff City (both twice) and Swansea and was also assistant manager at West Brom

I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth , and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.

Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.

We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.

"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."

That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!

It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.

I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.

It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.

I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.

It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.

Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.

Gibson appointed Pulis as Boro boss in December 2017. They reached the play-offs that season, then missed out on sixth place in the Championship by a single point in 2018-19

I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.

When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.

I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.

Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.

I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.

After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.

Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.

After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.

My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.

I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.

My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Erling Haaland has won two Premier League titles and three Premier League Golden Boots with Manchester City

It is a question many have asked but only a few have answered successfully. How do you stop Erling Haaland?

Wales will be faced with that daunting task when they travel to Oslo on Saturday to face Norway in the Nations League.

With a record 65 goals in just 59 games for his country – not to mention the hundreds he has scored for Manchester City and his previous clubs – Haaland has conquered most defences he has encountered.

But Wales managed to shackle him during their 2-1 win in Cardiff a month ago. In that sense, they have a blueprint to keep the fearsome striker at bay.

"You're talking about trying to deal with one of the best players in his position in the world, and we've been seeing that for several years now," says Wales head coach Craig Bellamy.

"He's different to what you would normally have to deal with. He has the profile of everything you want in a player, and that's quite rare.

"It's a collective responsibility, not just an individual one."

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Bellamy felt his team needed to take a calculated risk.

Some opponents have tried to sit back and defend deep against Haaland, but that can give him more time and space, more ways to wreak havoc.

Others have opted for a more confrontational, physical approach – not always wise against this powerful, 6ft 5in specimen.

Then there is the option of pressing high up the field. That can leave you exposed to balls over the top, which Haaland can race on to by using his raw pace.

Crucially, however, it can deny him – and, importantly, his talented team-mates – that time and space to inflict damage.

High-risk but high-reward, that is the route Bellamy chose.

"Drive up and don't let him dictate," he explains. "It's easier said than done because then you could turn around and say to me, 'Why are you playing a high line against Haaland?' Trust me you don't want to, but you can't have him dictating the game.

"That's true of all players, really, but it's much harder when someone is getting in your face and stopping you from having time on the ball.

"A good player can look like a top player if you give him time. A top player can look world-class if you give him time. A world-class player might then have a chance of looking like an ordinary or good player, if you don't allow him time.

"Putting pressure on the ball is always important for us, and I thought we did that really well that night."

Haaland was limited to 24 touches at Cardiff City Stadium. Anyone who has watched him play will know that is not unusual for the 26-year-old, who can drift in and out of a game around the pitch, only to come alive at key moments in the penalty area.

The more significant statistic is that he only had two shots, with only one on target, a header straight at Wales goalkeeper Danny Ward.

Prevention is better than a cure, and what Wales did effectively on that occasion was to cut off the supply of chances for Norway's talismanic frontman.

That was no mean feat considering that the Scandinavians' creator in chief is captain Martin Odegaard, one of the Premier League's most inventive playmakers and the man who led Arsenal to the title last season.

So as well as the defenders tasked with handling Haaland and his fellow forwards Fulham's Oscar Bobb and Andreas Schjelderup of Benfica, midfielders such as Ethan Ampadu had crucial roles to play in negating the attacking influence of Odegaard and his midfield colleagues.

"You have to consider the distance between Ethan and Haaland," Bellamy adds. "You can't open up the middle too much because balls are going to come into his feet. You have to get your distances right, be side-on and make sure you're aware of his runs.

"He has the ability to take a team on, but he also has the willingness to make those runs.

"It's also important how we use the ball. If we use it well, develop our possession and move up the pitch, he has to work. He has to run and get back."

Since Bellamy took charge in the summer of 2024, Wales' average share of possession in matches has rocketed.

They have had to make do with less of the ball in this Nations League campaign against Norway, Portugal and Denmark – and Bellamy believes his side could improve in that regard.

He has said Wales will be going "all out" for victory in Oslo on Saturday and, if they can stay on the front foot and make Norway defend, that is certainly one way of keeping Haaland out of the game.

"You have to be on it against these teams because they have many individual players who can create something out of nothing," says Dan James, who scored Wales' first goal in the 2-1 win.

"Our distances [between players] were really good. Odegaard is a unique player. He'll get the ball anywhere so it's hard as a defence. They want you to jump out and I think they showed that with their goal with the ball for Oscar Bobb and he's finished it well.

"We showed our resilience and it was about limiting their chances and I thought we did that.

"Odegaard played some great balls in behind but, to the very last minute, we defended really well, not just the defenders but the whole unit, from the forwards back.

"I thought we defended really well on the day, and we've got to be great again on Saturday."

Wales will be forced into at least one change in Oslo, with Swansea City centre-back Ben Cabango – who got Haaland's shirt after the game in Cardiff – missing through suspension.

The good news for Wales is that first-choice centre-back Joe Rodon, who was injured for the previous game, is available after returning for Leeds United last weekend.

"Ben Cabango and Ben Davies have both done really well against him [Haaland], but the work has to be done in front of them. If it isn't, you expose the defenders," Bellamy says.

"Against this type of player, it doesn't matter how good an individual defender is. We've seen over the last four or five years how difficult it becomes for one player to cope with what Haaland brings."

Taking on Haaland alone is not advisable. If you face the challenge together, however, as Wales showed just a month ago, you can stop the seemingly unstoppable.

MN202611_16e3sewwovq.t:
Blink-182 will be making their Download debut in 2027

Blink-182, Evanescence & Bring Me The Horizon have been announced as headliners of next year's Download Festival.

The trio are among more than 100 rock and metal acts set to play the event at Donington Park, Leicestershire from 9 to 13 June.

Other acts on the bill include The Prodigy, 5 Seconds of Summer and a special performance by heavy metal legends Mötley Crüe.

US pop-punk band Blink-182 will be making their Download debut, while Evanescence will become the festival's second female-fronted headliner.

The American rock band were founded by singer Amy Lee in the mid-1990s and had a UK number one with their best-known single Bring Me to Life in 2003.

It's the second year in a row a female-led band has headlined the festival, after Linkin Park topped the bill in 2025.

The nu-metal group have reformed with Emily Armstrong as their lead singer, after the death of former frontman Chester Bennington, who took his own life in 2017.

The choice of Emily upset some fans , who pointed to her alleged ties to the Church of Scientology and past support for convicted rapist Danny Masterson - someone she distanced herself from.

Amy Lee founded Evanescence more than 20 years ago

Next year's Download will be a first for Blink-182, who emerged from the California skate punk scene in the 1990s.

They've had two UK top 10 singles and had their first number one album in 2016, 21 years after their first record.

Their drummer Travis Barker is married to Kourtney Kardashian and survived a plane crash in the US that killed four people in 2008.

British rockers Bring Me The Horizon are more familiar to Download regulars, headlining for the second time in five years.

The four-piece band, formed in Sheffield, announced earlier this year they're celebrating 20 years of the debut album Count Your Blessings by re-recording it.

That 2006 record was in the deathcore genre, known for its heavy and aggressive sound, but the band have since moved towards metalcore, pop and electronic rock.

Some fans questioned if the original lyrics, which frontman Oli Sykes admitted could be interpreted as misogynistic, were still appropriate.

But the 39-year-old lead vocalist told the BBC Radio 1 Rock Show that going back to their roots was "a lot of fun" as they "got to remake the album how we wanted it to sound back then".

Bring Me the Horizon, fronted by Oli Sykes, headlined Reading and Leeds Festival last year

Download bills itself as a festival "spanning the full spectrum of rock, metal, punk, emo, hardcore, alternative and classic rock".

It called this year's line-up "bigger, better and bolder than ever" and said it features "something for everyone, from huge artists to electric newcomers".

But not everyone who commented on the festival's Instagram post was as convinced.

Writing about Blink-182, one person said "the fact they've been posted as some mega headliner at a metal festival blows my mind".

"Literally not one headliner that's proper metal," they added.

Fan Madison Travers, who's hoping to go to her ninth Download in a row, says she's "really happy with the line-up" - but thinks there's more to the festival.

"I don't think it matters about the line-up specifically," the 27-year-old tells Newsbeat.

"I think the community there and just the energy all weekend is what we look forward to."

Other acts announced include Turnstile, Faith No More, Body Count ft. Ice-T and Malevolence - with the festival saying more will be revealed.

Some pre-sales are currently available but tickets go on general sale at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.

In recent years Download has also featured pop acts and surprise guests, with the Vengaboys an unlikely addition to 2024's line-up.

And Dogstar - the band formed by actor Keanu Reeves - performed in 2026.

Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage

A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world.

Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced.

Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption.

Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.

Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue

Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries.

From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.

But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues.

As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.

The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".

In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.

"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.

Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".

In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.

Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".

The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.

When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.

Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.

Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.

"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.

"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.

"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.

"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."

The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".

He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.

Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.

"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.

In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.

Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.

In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.

The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.

Luke Graham (left) is being tipped for his first Scotland start - on the night Andy Robertson (right) could move level as the most-capped men's international

On Andy Robertson's night, it's difficult to not peek across the rest of the Scotland defensive line and worry.

The left-back will be lauded - whether he likes it or not - as he earns his 102nd cap, equalling Kenny Dalglish's men's record, against North Macedonia on Friday.

The captain is calling for it to be the King's night as much as his, and while the pair of Liverpool greats can have - and laugh - that out between them, the grace period for a giggle for Sebastien Pocognoli is petering out.

After an underwhelming opening camp, the head coach is in desperate need of a first home win - which he is hoping will come against the only side he's been victorious against in his opening four games.

The starting back three from that night in Skopje - Stephen Welsh, Scott McKenna and Luis Binks - are all out injured, forcing the Belgian to dig deep into the pool of central defenders, where he has pulled out a pair of names from the past in an attempt to arrest the porousness that plagued his debut international window.

Forgotten men Ryan Porteous and David Bates - the latter who last played international football seven years ago - join established but recent red card receiver Jack Hendry, and handful-of Scotland-minutes man Luke Graham as the centre-back quartet - but how much of a problem area is it already proving to be for Pocognoli?

Nations League: Scotland v North Macedonia

In comparison to the embarrassment of riches the head coach has in midfield and, more sparingly, in the forward areas, the heart of the back line is a bit bare.

Whoever slots alongside Tottenham Hotspur's Robertson - whether in Pocognoli's preferred back three, which could see Kieran Tierney shift in on the left side, or flat four - it's unlikely the combined caps haul of his centre-back buddies will come nearly close to his century plus.

The last of Los Angeles FC’s Porteous' 13 came against Greece in March 2025, while Bates picked up four under Alex McLeish six years before that.

Saudi Arabia-based Hendry is closing in on the half-century, while Celtic’s Tierney has surpassed it. Graham got a matter of minutes in North Macedonia after McKenna was dismissed.

Bates was playing in Germany with Hamburg when he faced Albania, Israel, Kazakhstan and San Marino and, after stints at a couple of clubs in Belgium, he's found himself with newly promoted albeit impressive Turkish Super Lig side Amedspor.

"There are a lot of players who are not available for the defensive line, but [David's] not there for nothing," Pocognoli said at Hampden Park on Thursday.

"He's there because he's performing well in Turkey with a team third in the rankings, in a tough competition."

Managed by Besnik Hasi - who played and managed in the Belgian's homeland - the head coach added: "I know the coach there as well, so I know he's also demanding a lot to the players.

"I can imagine the spirit in which he trains every day and I think for this camp, his experience can help some aspects on the pitch."

No excuses as Pocognoli seeks first Hampden victory

Robertson set to make history but his hero Dalglish will always be King

Dalkeith to LA pays off for Porteous with Scotland recall

Surely with no-one more so than Stoke City defender Graham, who has been tipped for a start by former England international Kevin Phillips.

Dundee's star performer last season has thrived for the Championship club this term - on the left of a back three - leaving many members of the Tartan Army deflated by the lack of minutes he was afforded last time out.

He came on after 88 minutes in the North Macedonian capital.

They might not be the only ones, too, given the in-form 22-year-old is now, surely, in pole position to face an under-firing North Macedonian front-line.

Friday's visitors have gone 12 games without a victory, failing to score in the latest eight and have lost their past five while conceding 14 goals.

They were "unlucky" to see the Swiss score three though, in Pocognoli's view. How he would take that scoreline in his side's favour now.

Victory is a near-must on matchday five. Sound and solid tactics, with a flavour of imagination and invention too wouldn't go amiss.

The latter qualities were seen as shortcomings of his predecessor, Steve Clarke, but stability in defence was a trademark of Clarke's tenure.

It's imperative Pocognoli picks up that mantle in his search for his first win at Hampden.

MN202611_lpeuv771lt.t:
Ngiyo imibare iheruka, mu bihumbi bimaze gutahuka mu Rwanda, kuva mu myaka ya za 1995, yakurikiye Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi n'ihunga ry'abarenga miliyoni eshatu, barimo abakoze Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi.

Mu bahunze icyo gihe harimo abagabo benshi, abana n'abagore. Bamwe barakuze, abandi barasaza, kandi bagiye bazira byinshi, harimo intambara zagiye zibera muri Congo, indwara z'ibyorezo n'inzara, n'ibindi binyuranye.

Abandi ariko na bo bagiye batahuka uko imyaka yagiye itambuka, ku buryo uwavuga ko abahunze benshi bamaze kagaruka mu rwababyaye, mu myaka isaga mirongo itatu ishize.

Icyakora, ikita rusange mu matsinda atahuka, nuko umubare munini uba ari uw'abana, uw'abagore ukaba mucye, hanyuma abagabo bakaba hafi ya ntabo.

Ikibazo gikomeye, cyabazwa FDLR, uyu mutwe w'iterabwoba wiganjemo abakoze Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi.

Ikigaragara, ni uko abagabo banga gutaha, ahubwo bakemerera abagore babo, n'abana babo bagataha iwabo.

Uwahamya ko baba baje ku bushake ashobora kuba wenda afite amakuru acagase, kuko biramutse ari ubushake, bakaba bazi ibyiza u Rwanda rubahishiye, simpamya ko umugabo yakwemera kohereza abamukomokaho, we agasigara mu mashyamba.

Ese ibyiza abagore n'abana baza kureba mu rwababyaye, abagabo babo baba babyanze, babisuzuguye cyangwa se, ingorane z'ishyamba baba bahunga, bo baba barazirenze, baba ari ibyuma?

Mu kiganiro bamwe mu bahoze mu buyobozi bwa FDLR bagoroye kuri KT Radio mu minsi ishize, bavuze ko FDLR idashaka gutaha, ndetse ko nta mugabo n'umwe ishaka ko ataha.

Uwo bemerera gutaha, ni umugabo warembye, babona ko atazakira, ameze nabi, atagishoboye kwiba, kurwana no kwica n'ibindi bibi.

Aha ariko, ngo babaha amabwiriza, avuga ko bagomba gutaha bakivuza - kuko FDLR ifite amakuru neza ko mu Rwanda ubuvuzi bwateye imbere - icyakora babongereraho bati "Nimugerayo, muzadukorera akazi k'ubutasi."

MN202611_kyc0lt4x2n.t:
Roseanna Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by US visa restrictions

Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.

Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.

"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.

Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.

"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.

In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.

"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.

Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.

The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.

Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.

"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.

Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."

In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.

She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"

The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

MN202611_1jfizpnax49.t:
Virgil van Dijk joined Liverpool for £75m from Southampton in January 2018

After Liverpool beat Brighton in October, Virgil van Dijk went upstairs to one of the hospitality lounges at Anfield and met up with Alan Hansen.

It was Van Dijk who, at the end of the 2024-25 season, asked the former Liverpool and Scotland defender to present him with the Premier League trophy and this time they posed for a picture that inevitably did the rounds on social media.

Whenever the time comes for Van Dijk to move on from Liverpool , he will go down as arguably their greatest centre-half, alongside Hansen. The question now is whether he will finish his career at Anfield like Hansen did in 1991.

Van Dijk's contract expires next summer and, even if the 35-year-old insisted this week that he was in no panic, it is a topic that will be a source of debate until a decision is made.

"Let's see what the season brings. I've had an amazing time already so far. If that will be extended, that's the case. If not, then I will go somewhere else," the Liverpool captain told reporters at Selhurst Park.

Two seasons ago, with Van Dijk in a similar situation, there was a similar sense of calm and come April 2025 he signed a two-year-deal.

Judging by Van Dijk's comments there is a feeling of him wanting to stay, but both he and Liverpool have an important decision to make.

Van Dijk and Alan Hansen are regarded as two of Liverpool's greatest defenders

Aside from a poor error against Villarreal in the Champions League, Van Dijk has shown this season that his standards haven't dropped.

His partnership with Jeremy Jacquet, who joined in the summer, is going from strength to strength and Van Dijk has played every minute in the Premier League since the start of last season.

A "little niggle" has affected him in recent weeks and this is the first international window he has missed with the Netherlands since Euro 2020, but it isn't a major cause for concern.

Liverpool have lost a number of senior figures in recent years but Van Dijk remains a leader in every form, and that was evidenced by his suggestion to Andoni Iraola that the squad should visit the museum at Anfield to learn more about the club's history.

At Crystal Palace on Sunday, it spoke volumes of Van Dijk's character that he came over to a group of reporters and asked if they wanted to speak to him, rather than the other way around. He regularly fronts up, regardless of the result.

Van Dijk is certainly not the force he was under Jurgen Klopp but he remains an elite centre-half and the stats justify that.

Per 90 minutes this season in the Premier League, he averages 60.7 successful passes per game, wins possession 3.5 times and makes 7.1 clearances. He has a 75% success in duels and 79% when it comes to aerial duels.

In his first full season at the club, in 2018-19, he averaged 72.4 successful passes per game, won possession 5.1 times and made 5.3 clearances. He had a 76% success in duels and 75% when it came to aerial duels.

That said, the Liverpool hierarchy will have seen the way the situation with Mohamed Salah unfolded last year and will be keen to avoid a repeat. After a stellar season in 2024-25, Salah's numbers plummeted in 2025-26.

Liverpool have a number of young centre-backs within their ranks, from Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni to the likes of Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye, but letting Van Dijk go would be a risk and leave a gaping hole.

He didn't take a pay cut in 2025 and continues to earn a salary understood to be in the region of £400,000 a week.

Joe Gomez, 29, is also out of contract this summer and Liverpool do have an option to buy Ronald Araujo, 27, at the end of the season from Barcelona but there would be a clear loss of experience and leadership if Van Dijk leaves.

For sporting director Julian Ward, the future of the Dutchman will be a priority over the coming months.

Providing he is fit, Van Dijk will make his 390th appearance for Liverpool when they take on Manchester United after the international break.

And given his consistency, he is likely to reach 400 appearances by the end of the year. He would become only the 28th Liverpool player to do so.

The 31 goals he has scored for Liverpool in the Premier League is the most for a defender at the club.

In terms of a resolution with his contract, this is likely to be one where both parties bide their time and, given that the existing relationships are strong and there's a mutual respect, it would not be a surprise to see negotiations go into 2027.

Come January, Van Dijk will be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club and as such, AC Milan and Juventus are monitoring the situation.

Sources in Turkey are also hopeful that they could tempt him to make the same move as Salah if an extension isn't agreed at Liverpool but, as it stands, it would be quite a surprise if Van Dijk moved on this summer.

The National Trust hopes to create new wildlife habitats to attract wildlife including water vole and turtle doves

A 370-acre (150-hectare) area of land on the edge of Cambridge has been returned to the care of the National Trust - for the first time in 60 years.

The area - known as Northfield - runs alongside the opposite side of Quy Road towards Bottisham, seven miles (11km) from the city and close to Anglesey Abbey.

The National Trust hopes to restore the natural site to create new wildlife habitats and improve community access to green space.

Emma Ormond-Bones, general manager of the National Trust's North Cambridgeshire Portfolio, said: "We want Northfield to become a place where nature can thrive, helping wildlife recover and building resilience to a changing climate."

The project comes at a time when Cambridgeshire remains one of the most nature-depleted counties in the UK, where demand for accessible green space is increasing as the county's population rapidly grows.

Northfield is a rich natural site with a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge

Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the tenants.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".

There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.

The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."

The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.

Community drop-in sessions about the vision , external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.

Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made her life "hell" at times

As a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.

At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.

Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.

As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable".

"Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.

Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts".

"I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.

Charlie didn't tell her parents about the severity of her condition for years

The condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.

Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.

Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.

The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".

But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.

It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits".

If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.

But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.

Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety".

"It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."

That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.

Charlie wants to raise awareness of the condition

A breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.

Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.

What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17.

"I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said.

"It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied.

"It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."

McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.

Niall McGonigle was inspired to become a surgeon after his experience with a pectus deformity

"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said.

"If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services.

"But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."

McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.

Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.

She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister.

"I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.

Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.

A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.

It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.

One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.

It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.

Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.

In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".

It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery".

"The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."

Vacuum bell therapy is a non-surgical treatment that works best for younger people

Last month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.

Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term.

"If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."
